title: Who Gets to Talk?
subtitle: How computers learned to share one wire without talking over each other.

pages.title: The Collision Problem & Pure ALOHA
pages.speaker: The Guide
pages.dialogue: When multiple hosts share one [[Shared Medium|shared-medium]], whether a copper cable or an open radio channel, transmitting simultaneously merges their signals into unreadable noise. In 1970, Norman Abramson designed ALOHAnet in Hawaii, linking island terminals over a shared inbound UHF radio channel. Under [[Pure ALOHA|pure-aloha]], any terminal transmits whenever ready and waits for a hub acknowledgment; if two bursts overlap by even a single bit across a two-packet window, both garble and retry after random timeouts, capping channel efficiency at 18.4 percent.

deepDive.title: Pure Aloha
deepDive.focus: Derives Pure ALOHA's 2T vulnerable window, collision retries, and 18.4% peak throughput.

pages.title: Slotted ALOHA: Taming the Clock
pages.speaker: The Guide
pages.dialogue: Pure ALOHA wasted bandwidth because a late packet could clip the tail of an earlier one already mid-flight. In 1972, Lawrence Roberts introduced [[Slotted ALOHA|slotted-aloha]], dividing time into synchronized discrete slots equal to one packet duration. Terminals may only begin transmitting at the exact tick of a new slot boundary, shrinking the vulnerable overlap window in half and doubling peak throughput to 36.8 percent. Yet blind radios still cannot hear each other mid-air, so two stations picking the same tick still ruin an entire slot.

pages.title: Ethernet's Shared Coax & CSMA/CD
pages.speaker: The Guide
pages.dialogue: In May 1973 at Xerox PARC, Bob Metcalfe and David Boggs needed to wire dozens of Alto workstations to one fast laser printer without a fragile central switch. They ran a single passive [[Coaxial Ether|coaxial-ether]] cable tapped by every machine and paired it with [[CSMA/CD|csma-cd]]. Each transceiver listens for carrier voltage before sending, then monitors the wire while transmitting; if two signals collide, the summed voltage triggers an instant abort and a short jam signal so every host stops wasting wire time immediately.

They ran a single passive Coaxial Ether cable tapped by every machine and paired it with CSMA/CD. Each transceiver listens for carrier voltage before sending, then monitors the wire while transmitting; if two signals collide, the summed voltage triggers an instant abort and a short jam signal so every host stops wasting wire time immediately.
pages.sceneNotes: Passive 50-ohm terminated coax bus links Alto A, Alto B, and the EARS laser printer via transceiver taps above a live voltage strip. Alto B defers while sensing Alto A's carrier, then both transmit together, spiking summed collision voltage in crimson to trigger an instant abort and jagged jam signal.

pages.title: Binary Exponential Backoff
pages.speaker: The Guide
pages.dialogue: Aborting a collision only works if both stations do not immediately retransmit in lockstep and collide forever. Ethernet breaks the tie with [[Binary Exponential Backoff|binary-exponential-backoff]]. After its first collision, each host flips a coin to wait zero or one slot time; after the second collision, it picks randomly from zero to three slots, doubling the contention window on each clash up to 1,023 slots. That self-tuning spread lets busy offices sustain over eighty percent link utilization without a master clock, though heavy bursts still spike latency.

pages.sceneNotes: Host A and Host B state cards feed a contention-window ladder (k=1: 0..1, k=2: 0..3, k=3: 0..7) above a shared wire. Both pick slot 0 on clash 1 and collide again; on clash 2 the window doubles so Host A picks slot 1 and transmits cleanly before Host B follows on slot 3, pushing utilization past 80%.

pages.title: Ethernet Frames & 48-Bit MAC Addresses
pages.speaker: The Guide
pages.dialogue: Because a passive wire broadcasts every electrical pulse to every tap, each host needs hardware rules to separate valid messages from background traffic. Standardized by DIX in 1980 and IEEE 802.3 in 1983, an [[Ethernet Frame|ethernet-frame]] opens with a synchronizing preamble, stamps 48-bit destination and source [[MAC Address|mac-address]] headers, pads short payloads to 64 bytes so distant collisions propagate back in time, and appends a 32-bit CRC checksum. Network cards silently filter unmatched addresses in silicon, keeping CPUs free for real work.

Network cards silently filter unmatched addresses in silicon, keeping CPUs free for real work.
pages.sceneNotes: Annotated Ethernet Frame blueprint splits PREAMBLE + SFD (8B), DST MAC (6B), SRC MAC (6B), TYPE / LEN (2B), PAYLOAD + PAD (46–1500B), and CRC-32 FCS (4B), with an explicit lower bracket spanning DST MAC through CRC-32 FCS labeled >=64B MIN FRAME (512 BITS). Below, a broadcast frame is silently dropped by unmatched NICs and accepted by the matching MAC after CRC verification.

pages.title: 1983 IEEE 802.3 & The Next Crisis
pages.speaker: The Guide
pages.dialogue: By 1983, IEEE 802.3 turned local office wiring into a global standard, though packing dozens of hosts into one shared [[Collision Domain|collision-domain]] still strained busy rooms until switches later gave every port its own wire. Even then, Ethernet's success exposed a bigger barrier: a flat 48-bit MAC address only identifies a card on one local cable, carrying zero map of the outside world. With Ethernet LANs, ARPANET trunks, and packet radio all speaking incompatible frames, how do you bridge separate networks into one global Internet?

shared-medium.plainEnglish: A single physical communication channel—such as a coaxial bus cable or a shared radio frequency band—whose bandwidth is accessed directly by multiple transmitters rather than dedicated point-to-point wires.
shared-medium.whyItWasInvented: Running a private point-to-point cable between every pair of computers in a building or across islands scales quadratically in cost and wiring complexity, so engineers pooled hosts onto one shared channel.
shared-medium.realWorldSighting: Every Wi-Fi radio channel, neighborhood DOCSIS cable broadband trunk, and passive GPON fiber splitter still forces multiple customer devices to take turns across one shared physical medium.

pure-aloha.plainEnglish: A decentralized random-access protocol where any station transmits a packet immediately whenever data is ready, waits for an acknowledgment from the receiver, and retries after a random timeout if a collision corrupts it.
pure-aloha.whyItWasInvented: Norman Abramson's University of Hawaii team needed remote island terminals to send bursty keyboard traffic over one UHF radio channel without expensive leased telephone lines or a rigid polling scheduler.
pure-aloha.realWorldSighting: Low-power LoRaWAN Class A IoT sensors and simple unslotted telemetry beacons still transmit using unslotted Pure ALOHA bursts whenever strict clock synchronization would drain battery life.

slotted-aloha.plainEnglish: A time-synchronized upgrade to Pure ALOHA that divides the channel into uniform packet-length clock ticks so stations only start sending at slot boundaries, halving the vulnerable collision window from two packet times to one.
slotted-aloha.whyItWasInvented: Lawrence Roberts showed that unaligned transmissions let a newly starting packet destroy an almost-finished packet; aligning starts onto discrete boundaries immediately doubled maximum channel throughput from 18.4% to 36.8%.
slotted-aloha.realWorldSighting: Modern 4G LTE and 5G smartphones still use slotted random-access preambles on the PRACH channel whenever waking up to request an initial uplink slot from a cellular base station.

coaxial-ether.plainEnglish: A passive, shielded copper coaxial cable terminated at both ends with 50-ohm resistors to absorb signal reflections, allowing stations to clip directly onto the shared bus via transceiver taps without an active central switch.
coaxial-ether.whyItWasInvented: Xerox PARC engineers needed a reliable multi-megabit office network linking Alto computers to a high-speed laser printer where any single workstation could fail or unplug without bringing down the rest of the room.
coaxial-ether.realWorldSighting: Offices eventually replaced shared coaxial thicknet buses with twisted-pair RJ45 cables wired into gigabit switches, while shielded coaxial cable still delivers high-frequency DOCSIS broadband into millions of homes.

csma-cd.plainEnglish: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: stations listen for an idle wire before sending, monitor voltage while transmitting to spot collisions instantly, broadcast a 32-bit jam pattern, and abort early instead of finishing corrupted frames.
csma-cd.whyItWasInvented: Blind ALOHA radios wasted entire packet durations transmitting over already-garbled collisions; tapping a wired coax cable let Ethernet transceivers detect clashes in microseconds and reclaim wasted bandwidth immediately.
csma-cd.realWorldSighting: Full-duplex gigabit Ethernet switches eliminated collisions on modern wired LANs, while Wi-Fi relies on its wireless descendant CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance) because radios cannot easily listen while broadcasting on the same frequency.

binary-exponential-backoff.plainEnglish: A randomized retry algorithm where each colliding station picks a random waiting count from 0 to 2^k - 1 slot times after its k-th collision, doubling the contention window on each clash up to 0 to 1,023 slots (aborting after 16 retries).
binary-exponential-backoff.whyItWasInvented: Fixed retry timers cause two colliding hosts to keep clashing in lockstep forever; dynamically widening a randomized window automatically adapts to how many stations are competing at that exact instant.
binary-exponential-backoff.realWorldSighting: Wi-Fi contention windows, cloud API client SDKs, and distributed database reconnect loops all use exponential backoff with random jitter to prevent synchronized retry storms from crushing overloaded servers.

ethernet-frame.plainEnglish: A structured Layer-2 container wrapping payload bytes with an 8-byte synchronizing preamble and start delimiter, 48-bit destination and source MAC headers, a 2-byte EtherType or length field, padding to 64 bytes minimum, and a 32-bit CRC checksum.
ethernet-frame.whyItWasInvented: Raw voltage transitions on a shared broadcast wire provide no message boundaries, recipient filters, or noise verification; standardized framing ensured cards from DEC, Intel, Xerox, and every IEEE 802.3 vendor interoperated cleanly.
ethernet-frame.realWorldSighting: Capture live traffic in Wireshark and expand the Ethernet II header on any packet to see its destination MAC, source MAC, and EtherType field—such as 0x0800 for IPv4 or 0x86DD for IPv6.

mac-address.plainEnglish: A globally unique 48-bit hardware identifier written as six hexadecimal pairs—combining a 24-bit IEEE manufacturer prefix with a 24-bit device serial—burned into each network interface card for local Layer-2 addressing.
mac-address.whyItWasInvented: On a shared broadcast cable where every transceiver receives every frame, network cards needed a permanent hardware label to accept only matching frames in silicon without interrupting the host CPU.
mac-address.realWorldSighting: Run ip link or ipconfig /all to inspect your device's MAC address; enterprise gigabit switches inspect those headers to build live MAC address tables mapping each device to its physical RJ45 port.

collision-domain.plainEnglish: The electrical boundary of a local network segment within which two devices transmitting at the exact same instant physically interfere with each other's signals and trigger a collision.
collision-domain.whyItWasInvented: As offices grew from ten workstations to hundreds on shared coaxial cables and passive hubs, engineers needed a precise term for the contention bottleneck limiting aggregate throughput and motivating bridge and switch segmentation.
collision-domain.realWorldSighting: Modern gigabit Ethernet switches give every RJ45 port its own dedicated full-duplex link with separate send and receive paths, disabling CSMA/CD and eliminating wired collision domains completely.
